Plus, in every room they have nice flat screen TV's so a weary traveler can catch up on the news and daily events. The hostess took us to the room in the back section of the establishment where everyone else seemed to be seated. It looked as if there was only one server on at this time a day, but you couldn't tell due to the attention of the service. As soon as we were seated she came by to say hi and to take our drink order, and to ask if we were ready. As usual we weren't so she gave us our time to see what we wanted. They have the normal diner foods like your traditional breakfasts, that one can get all day. They also serve both cold and hot sandwiches, which includes your burger selections, plus their dinner sections, which features seafood, steaks, poultry, and pasta dishes. My buddy got a meatball sub, which I'm guessing he liked since it disappeared fast. I decided on a tuna club, but I don't like lettuce and tomatoes. All I really wanted was the tuna, cheese, and, most importantly, the bacon. Usually I just put the veggies to the side, put the bacon and cheese between two pieces of bread, and then add the tuna between the other piece. Knowing times are kinda tough and every restaurant is looking for ways to save money, believe me every piece of lettuce adds up, I tell the waitress to hold those items. She does one better. She suggests that I got what's called a shorty. Basically it's what I wanted minus the third piece of bread. She also informed me that this saves me a little money to. I found this to be a particularly awesome trait in a server, who most of the time is trying to raise the check to get a bigger tip. I know they are told to upsell certain items but in this case it saved both me and probably the diner some cash. Both dishes were served with a side of fries and I believe cole slaw, not sure though about the slaw. I really can't comment on my friend's meat ball sandwich. All he said was that it was good. I know, very descriptive, huh? Mine, on the other hand, was a perfect sandwich. I enjoyed not having the extra stuff I didn't want cluttering up my plate, plus the fries were nice and crunchy, which is just the way I like them. We finished up, paid the bill and went on our way. I can definitely say Penns Queen Diner is fat kid tested fat kid approved. As always Stay peckish my friends.

text: Come to Mother's restaurant to get some real home-cooked Southern dishes! After watching Adam Richman from Man vs. Food pay a visit and eat a juicy Po-Boy - I just had to try it! YES - there is ALWAYS a line and its always LONG. But suck it up - because it goes pretty fast. I'd say we had at least 30 people in front of us and we were in within 15 min. Why? The restaurant inside is HUGE (self-seating) and the line to order your food inside is basically the only bottle neck. --Famous Fredi's Special ($11.75)-- MUST TRY! This is what Mother's is known for! This sandwich is basically a huge pile of meat all placed between a french roll (which is also dipped in meat juice)! SO hearty and satisfying! What kinds of meat you ask? A variety: black ham, thick slices of roast beef, and of course the DEBRIS! When they described it on Man vs. Food - I was a little disturbed. The bits and pieces of left over meat - how can that be good? IT IS! TRUST! Its like a juicier version of pulled pork - soft and slow cooked! Make sure you get a stack of napkins - because this sandwich can get MESSY. With the meat juice, shredded cabbage, globs of mayo + mustard, gravy, and of course the layers of meat, you will have to wipe with each bite. All the meat went really well with the tangy and yet creamy sauces - I went to carnivore heaven! --Jerry's Omelete ($11)-- After feeling a little sickly from all the heavy meals in NOLA - I ordered an egg white omelete in hopes of giving my poor stomach a break. The omelete was filled with bell pepper, turkey, red onions, and mushrooms. This was the blandest plate of food ever! I had to salt + pepper with each bite! Not only that, the topping to egg proportion was too little and the entire plate was covered in grease! I did enjoy the taste of grits - which I'm not used to! Felt like home in my belly! :) I also got to try Mother's famous jam with my toast.. but all in all, this is a dish to avoid. --Combination Platter ($19)-- Yes we're tourists and we want to taste everything. So what better way than to order the combo platter which comes with Jerry's Jambalaya, etouffee, red beans, vegetables, and potato salad!? This plate is a blessing because you do get to try so many dishes - but after tasting these same dishes elsewhere in NOLA, I can tell you this combination platter may not be worth it. A lot of the food @ Mother's just tasted really mushy, goopy, and a little bland. The etouffee was one shining star on the dish - which was very flavorful. I think one downfall of this dish is that all these dishes are plopped onto the same tiny plate and the flavors get lost in the mix! --Mae's Gumbo Cup ($6)-- A small little cup of gumbo - which tasted homey and less salty than other places. But I honestly had a hard time differentiating the different gumbos at the variety of NOLA restaurants. Meh - nothing special. Tips 1) Self seating area is much bigger in Mother's next door 2) Soft drink ($2.25) - unlimited refills 3) FREDI'S SPECIAL!

This place is a straight forward burger joint. It's what they do. Sure you can get a chili/cheese dog or even a grilled cheese sandwich, but the burger is the main event here! Unless you order the "little" burger, all burgers are double-burgers. You can get them with an impressive list of ingredients available, to customize your burger and make it patently yours! I love the grilled onions and jalapeño peppers! But you can get other "fix in's" such as grilled 'shrooms, green peppers, even A-1 Steak Sauce! They offer Cajun seasoned fries. From my perspective, they are tasty, but a little on the salty side. So if you have blood pressure issues, buyer beware! A note about their fries though... they sell two sizes; regular and large. Trust me, the regular is plenty. My family of five, can get two regular orders, and they are more than enough. They really overload them! So if you're really into fries, go for it. But don't say I didn't want you! Pretty simple review, but that's really the extent of it. Five Guys does burgers and they do 'em well. If you're in the mood, you can't go wrong here.

text: The interior of this space is almost unrecognizable to anyone who frequented the former Cooper's on Porter. Gone is the wall behind the bar, which now opens to show inside the kitchen. The weird booths in the middle that segmented the restaurant have been replaced by two brick columns, which gives it a much more open feel. We sat in the back, where an open garage door overlooks the patio, allowing in the fresh air while still keeping us out the rain. Their menu design needs a little work, but they have an impressive wine list, though more bottles than by the glass, and several beers in bottles, though only two drafts. We didn't get an appetizer, though they had a nice selection plus a special not on the menu. Instead, we split a Caesar salad. The dressing was really light despite coating the lettuce entirely, but could have used a little extra oomph. The croutons were made from the same bread we were served with olive oil -- nice and garlicky. Speaking of garlic, let's get to the entrees. I ordered the half portion of the potato-suffed ravioli with crawfish tails, butter and lemon. Very flavorful, with a nice garlic-laden broth of some sort as a sauce. The crawfish tails were huge, very shrimplike for what I'm used to (I'm from around here, so growing up I ate my share of "crawdaddies" that didn't resemble these at all), and the potato filling in the ravioli was basically creamy mashed potatoes -- smoother than the consistency of the usual ricotta. The ravioli was slightly undercooked on the edges, but I still inhaled it. And a great deal for only $9 ($17 for a full portion). He tried the pizza with lamb sausage, fennel, tomatoes and arugula. Not too crusty, but not cracker-thin (we both prefer a crust on the thinner side), and generous with the toppings, though a little skimpy on the sauce, but that may be their style. No complaints -- and at $11, a decent deal for gourmet pizza. We arrived around 6:30 on a Friday night and were sat immediately, though probably just in the nick of time, since there was a huge line out the door when we left. As far as service goes (since I've seen complaints), our drinks took a while to arrive, but our server was very apologetic. And at least two other people (owners?) stopped by during the course of our meal to ask how everything was -- I imagine they just want to make a good first impression, which they certainly did. When our food didn't arrive as soon as she had promised, our server offered to buy us a second round of drinks, even though we weren't complaining. And then our food arrived immediately after that. So ... free drinks for not-really-that-slow service? I'll definitely be back. Although to second another reviewer... where was the hostess stand? And more importantly, this place needs a website, or at the very least a Facebook page. I know it's owned by the same folks who run Eastland Cafe, so I figure they are just trying to do a soft opening for a few weeks before they start heavy promotions, but if it weren't for a food blogger posting about them, I wouldn't have known they were open.

text: Excellent food, best draft beer selection downtown, and a unique space. I've been four times in the first week, and I've been very impressed by how far it's come in such a short amount of time. I'm a little baffled by some of the reviews that describe the portions as too small. On the contrary, I've never left without my gut stuffed. If you're going with one other person, splitting a pizza and a salad is a perfect lunch serving. The pasta servings are also quite generous, and they don't skimp on the meat. Considering the quality of the food and the portions, I think the value is actually quite good. The pizza itself features some of the best crust in Tucson. In their first couple days, there was some inconsistency with the dough that resulted in the occasional overly thick pizza. Fortunately, on my last two visits, the crust was excellent: crunchy, slightly charred, with just the right amount of salt. The pizza options are split between several tomato sauce-based pies and a few "white" options with panna or olive oil. The salami and roasted fresno is my early favorite, with just enough heat to cut through the mozzarella and fontina. There's also a vegan pizza, along with a few solid vegetarian options. Though pizza is the focus at Reilly, I was very impressed by the two pasta dishes I tried (Papardelle with braised short ribs and Cavatelli with fennel sausage). The pasta is made fresh daily, and you can tell. It's easy to forget, but skillfully made pasta makes a world of difference. The chef, Tyler Fenton, worked under Daniel Scordato at Vivace, Tucson's best Italian restaurant, so he knows how to execute a great pasta dish. Like most of the menu, the salads are a great representation of the harmonious marriage between the classic and the modern on display at Reilly. For instance their version of a "caesar" salad (they even put the quotation marks on the menu) jazzes up the traditional caesar by adding Kale and polenta croutons. Instead of simply drizzling balsamic on the caprese, they use balsamic "caviar" (essentially, small gelatinous balls of balsamic vinegar). Though the salads are a touch small to be a full meal, they can easily be split between two people as a starter. The bar has an excellent selection of craft beer on tap, with a focus on west coast breweries. They also have an impressive array of draft wine selections and a full list of craft cocktails. The space itself is open and airy, with a host of unique touches. The atmosphere is stylish but unpretentious, and it would be appropriate for everything from a first date to a large family gathering. All in all, I'm thrilled to have Reilly as a new downtown option. It's especially nice to have another late night dining option downtown. I'll certainly be a regular, and I'm eager to see how it continues to grow and improve.

text: Living in three separate regions of France for the past four year, I've gotten to know the in's and out's of typical French snack cuisine. I've tried an array of French sandwiches, quiches, pastries, and desserts. And usually after being in any one neighborhood long enough, you begin to sort out who offers the best mouth-watering croissants versus the places whose baguettes are better apt to be sponges. Moving back to the Philadelphia for a few months last year, I went mad searching for the perfect baguette - squeezing each one at the various locations anticipating that beautiful crunch sound that comes with the most delicious of baguettes but was disappointed to discover that 9/10 bakeries (in fact all of Philadelphia's well-known bakeries from Whole Foods to Miel) boasting "French Baguettes" were merely offering a horrible impostor [Rouge and this shady, dark little place off the main street of Chestnut Hill so far offer the best of the best baguettes]. So to the critic who gave Art of Bread 5 stars and claims no one on here knows real French food, well now we know someone on here does. I was looking forward to Art of Bread - A place for me to get my French-Fix while visiting Philadelphia and, God willing, a haven for the authentic French baguette. After all, if there is anyone able to bring it to Philadelphia, it should be Perrier. But my heart sank when I pulled up to the little café. Already it looks like a glorified chain rather than a Perrier creation for fine French food. Inside it was chaotic. It wasn't clear where the line was nor what to do once you ordered. The employees behind the counter where frazzled - the girl trying to take my order was constantly being interrupted by a bossy girl always telling her it would be better if "you say this, say that." The girl taking my order was doing fine and I understood exactly what she was trying to explain - the impromptu coaching was unprofessional and made my experience more annoying with each interruption. Not to mention the irritating guy at the pick-up counter that kept yelling things across the room and shouting out to customers, getting their attention with smart ass quips like "Hey, girl in the black top." And then there was the food... my "Crazy Chicken" looked horrible. Oily toasted bread pilled hight with gloppy cheese and hardly any chicken. It didn't resemble any of the French tartines I've seen before and while it tasted ok, I could only eat half because of the amount of grease. The eclair I had as my dessert that came with the already unhealthy lunch was by far one of the worst I've had - the only good think about it was the little tuff of gold on top. I'll be back one more time to try their coffee, croissants and bring home a baguette for dinner (I'll be squeezing it first thing! ;) ). While my hopes are not high, I at least hope that the employees will have learned a thing or two about running the show behind the counter, working together respectfully and as a team, all the while treating the customer with the utmost respect (despite customer service not being France's strong suit). I understand Art of Bread has a completely different purpose than any of Perrier's other ventures and is targeting hurried business professionals on their short lunch breaks but Art of Bread should have been and still could be so much more.

text: After reading good reviews, we decided to check out Ernesto's on a Wednesday night. The waiter informed us about the 1/2 price bottle deal and we ordered an okay, drinkable Rioja but that was the end of the pleasant experience. The decor is nice but there is no noise control, so it's not a relaxed environment. After half an hour, our disappointing flatbread arrived (frozen food is better). Another hour later, the next part of our order arrived - a forgettable small cheese plate and a rancid beef dish we had to send back (something we never do). Our bar seats allowed us direct view of the shell-shocked appearing, snail paced chef. We will never return. In fact, we had to grab dinner after this meal. This may be a cute place to grab a drink if you're in the neighborhood but the charm ends there. It certainly has potential if they overhaul the dining portion.

We tried two of their cocktail offerings. A vodka and ginger concoction and the Manzanilla, a tequila and apple cider mix. Both were very nice served in martini glasses and very cold. The service was very nice and all in all it was a lovely way to ease into a hot New Orleans weekend.

text: Racial discrimination in 2012? Really? Really. My boyfriend and I, who is African American, went to Chez Leon for a nice date all dressed up and ready to enjoy some wonderful food. The owner sat us apprehensively and without a word. Our server came five minutes later asking us what we will have to drink without offering any wine list, without welcoming us, or telling us his name, or the whole intro schpiel that all the other tables got. Other patrons were served very well: water topped off, bread served, the menu and specials described, friendly chatter from the server, wine lists offered, and meal suggestions given when asked. Not to mention served promptly and asked if their food was liked. We are not high expectation guests but NONE of this was offered to us. We were visited by our server a total of one time in the 40 mins it took for us to decide to leave. In fact for some reason we were smirked at and laughed at when asking our server his recommendations. It was made plain to us upon walking in we were not welcome. We were tastefully dressed and friendly. Unfortunately I can only assume we fell victim to the staff's prejudices towards African Americans. My S.O. and I have been together 3+ years and never have we felt so unwelcome, uncomfortable, and unwanted in any setting, much less a restaurant where we were happy to pay for a fine dining experience.
label: NEG

text: I have started a weekly "dining club" with a friend of mine, and last week we picked Cafe Tiramisu to dine out. Seeing as how we work just downward on High Street, it was nice to stay in the neighborhood and see a new business in a thriving community. The space is gorgeous and open - which a little separate room for kids and lots of bright pieces of furniture. Even though it does look like a cafe - they do offer table service, which is nice. The service was fine and attentive, but the food was rather sub-par, unfortunately. I had a pasta dish, which was just so-so, overcooked and kind of flavorless. I chose the Tiramisu for dessert, but it was super heavy and rich and not my favorite - I guess I prefer my tiramisu a little lighter. The smoothie I had was by far the best part of my meal - super flavorful and delicious (too bad I hadn't just gone for that). One of my biggest complaints about this space is the NOISE. It was fairly busy when we were there, but the place wasn't jam packed - but you never would have known because you couldn't hear a damn thing. It was useless trying to have a conversation with my friend, who was sitting directly across from me, because we couldn't hear a single word each other was saying without screaming. It was distracting and just.... not comfortable. I guess it was the acoustics, or how close the tables were seated. I'm not sure, but it was just not a great place to sit down and have a meal. Unfortunately, with a poor dining atmosphere and mediocre food, I'm not really anticipating revisiting Cafe Tiramisu. Unless of course, I'm in the mood for a smoothie. Then maybe... just maybe... I'll go back. Maybe.

text: My friend and I managed to grab a last-minute reservation here on a Sunday and both opted for the prix fixe menu. Bibou, you were excellent from start to finish. The meal started off with a salted cod soup was out of this world! It went great with the free breadsticks that we got. On to the appetizers. I got the escargot; the snails tasted like perfectly seasoned mushrooms. My friend's foie gras was very fatty though. Not for me. But the sauce that came with it was unique and flavorful. I had the halibut for the entree and it was cooked very well, but it didn't pack a punch. I can't blame the chef because halibut does not have a lot of flavor to begin with. What I really loved was the arctic char dumpling, which was baked to perfection and complemented with a wonderfully creamy tomato sauce. It also came with a side of red rice, which was also very nice. For dessert, I chose the floating island while my friend chose the creme brulee with honey and rosemary. The floating island was really light and a perfect finish to my meal. I liked that the creme brulee wasn't very sweet because it would have contrasted so much with the other courses on the menu. The cherry on top was when the chef came out and took his time to talk to everyone. It really made me feel at home and I was very touched. Overall a stellar dining experience: I can see myself coming back here again and again.

I ordered the tomato, basil, & mozzarella panini and took a seat in the dining area. My sandwich arrived- a decent size, along with a plate full of potato chips and a pickle on the side. The first few bites of the sandwich tasted delicious - perhaps because I was starving.. However, after I got over my hunger I couldn't help but notice how greasy my sandwich was, more like a grilled cheese sandwich than a panini. Despite the greasiness, I finished the sandwich and overall the lunch was ok. The dining room was quiet and clean, service was passable, and the food was tasty (minus the greasy bread). I'll probably explore other options next time I'm in suburban square.

The breadbowl tasted stale, like it had been taken out of a fridge and reheated in the microwave. I finished the soup because I was hungry but just left the bowl to sit there. Charlie got a caesar salad, which was just some lettuce with cheese and croutons sprinkled on top. The lettuce was slimy and the croutons were soggy by the time they were brought to the table. The service was friendly and the prices weren't expensive, but the food was absolutely abysmal. Don't waste your money--stick with Bread Co.

House salad is filling and comes in a really neat pink-colored Greek dressing. Lamb chops are superb, but if you are on a budget, the gyro entree is awesome. For $14, you get the salad, bread, and then a gigantic plate with the gyro, and Santorini's 3 classic sides, rice pilaf, beans, and lemon potatoes. text: I was REALLY excited to finally check out Edley's after hearing numerous rave reviews about the joint. I can't lie - I was pretty disappointed. FOOD - the options all sound delicious, but nothing really won me over. The mac and cheese was too bland and peppery, the bean salad was tasty, but too watery and while the pulled pork sandwich was DELICIOUS, it wasn't anything to write home about. DRINK - drink options seemed well enough, but I think it was kinda pricey. The bar is pretty small. You place your order in one place and then have to walk over, squeeze your way in-between people sitting at the bar to get your beer. A little awkward. ATMOSPHERE - it was okay. I'll bet it becomes a BIG hangout in the spring, though, when the patio can be put to use and the garage doors are pulled up. It felt like a typical BBQ joint on the inside - already a bit sticky and dirty. SERVICE - I actually liked the service the best. The girl who took my order was friendly and helpful - she even gave me a small sample of the bean salad to decide to order it. I did have some trouble tracking down additional sauce for my pulled pork sandwich, but a server helped me locate one. Overall, I'll probably go again because I love the 12 South neighborhood and that patio will be excellent in the warmer months, but I probably won't be the one to recommend we hit it up.

text: This is a pleasant change from the commercial, nice, neat and sort of impersonal settings of most big hotel chains like Hilton or Marriott. The breakfast that is included with the room is served in the hotel lobby and the hostess greets you like family. Soon you find yourself talking to other guests and exchanging your emails. The breakfast is continental, what most of really eat when we're home, and always fresh and welcome. In the afternoon, wonderful large chocolate chip cookies are served in the lobby and fresh fruit is available all day long. The Inn itself is a block of so from the beach and also a short walk from Santa Barbara's Amtrack station and its most charming business district. The staff here knows something about absolutely everything in or near Santa Barbara and are very helpful to the traveler. Because the inn is well established, the landscaping is mature and very attractive and the entire experience is worth the modest cost. It's charming, cozy, well-priced, well-located, friendly and really feels a little like going back to grandma's house for a holiday vacation.

text: Yowzers!! Is this place still in business?! How can I plead mighty Odin to strike down this New Orleans tragedy?? Look, let's get something straight....I'm all for stimulating local business, especially the New Orleans restaurant market. I've tried several times to give this place a chance and yet, it continues to teeter between 'not quite adequate' and 'downright deplorable'. The last time I dined in there, a wave of horrible past experiences came over me. Perhaps the gods were trying to communicate with me that something was amiss. I should have just asked the hostess kindly if this was the entryway into the first level of Dante's Inferno. Joking aside, here's how the last trip had gone down. I entered the burning ring of fire a.k.a. walkway into 5 Fifty 5 and the hostess seated us around the back of the restaurant in a dark corner, almost shutting us off from any other human contact. Realistically speaking, we were only the second dinner party in the place. I saw another couple sitting about 4 or 5 tables away. I glanced over and as the man drew his spoon to his mouth to sip his soup, his head chillingly turned in my direction, his eyes piercing me in a unnerving manner; his mouth curled upward into a grim smile as if he, too, knew what I was in for. Boy, I should have left at that very moment. We put in an order for drinks....mojitos, I believe they were. The drinks were very good. I will have to say that whoever the bartender was, they knew their craft. Over the course of our duration, we ordered a number of various drinks and they were all satisfying. That is the end of the 'happy' portion of this perilous tale, however. For starters, I ordered the fried calamari. I love a restaurant that showcases a great calamari dish. I had some great calamari at this joint on St. Charles Ave. in the CBD called 'The Cobalt' but alas, it fell victim to Katrina. It is now the home of John Besh's 'Restaurant Luke'. Anyway, after some time waiting, the calamari arrived....and what a frightening scene it was. In all cases of calamari I have ordered, you get little ringlets or something of that nature. In this experience, however, what I had were whole squid bodies, some that didn't even appear to be cooked the whole way through; their limbs stretching outward, as if reaching for help from the fryer below them. I had to look away. It was like peering at those ash casts of Pompeii victims during the volcanic blast of Vesuvius in 79 A.D. Ugh!! Next, came the entrée and I was praying, fingers crossed under the table that my main course wouldn't arrive in such a terrifying fashion. I had ordered the halibut in a butter sauce with a bit of a what resembled cheese grits. First, the halibut was severely over cooked. I mean, there was literally a shell of burned meat around the fish so that had to be discarded. The butter was so IMMENSLEY over salted. Ever gone swimming at the beach and accidently taken a wave to the face when your mouth was open? Remember the puckering of salinity? That's how bad this sauce was. I couldn't eat anything that touched it....or even got within proximity. Everything else that came with my dish, strangely, was bland. Now, how can you absolutely torch a great cut of halibut and mix in seawater with your cream sauce but skip everything else? Was the salt content of the sauce supposed to make up for the lack of flavors in everything else or that they turned my halibut into beef jerky? As the late Macho Man Randy Savage used to cry out: "snap into a Slim Jim!" Now, on to my guest's meal: I'm not sure it's available on the menu anymore as I just checked the restaurant's website and the item is missing. In any case, they ordered the sea bass and a rice concoction of pineapple juice and some sort of cream sauce. The sea bass was also devoid of anything resembling flavor however, the side of rice pudding (??) was good. Now, I don't mind eating at a nice restaurant and spending money for good food. This was anything BUT good, though. THE best thing about our meal was the drinks and if I wanted that, I would have just stayed at the bar! The reason I decided on dining here was because the place was promoting like crazy, Gambit wrote up a glowing review about the courses available and the wizardry skills of the head chef. The Gambit columnist obviously didn't order what I ordered. I'll never forget that meal. It was ghastlier than 1,000 ghouls! This is a cautionary tale for the rest of you, folks!! Steer clear!!

text: here we go again: disorganized staff, a bit chaotic layout, not much atmosphere and well planned menu which served up bland and tasteless food. Sounds like a lot of St. Louis restaurants, though Nico should know better because Franco, the older brother, seems to be chugging along quite nicely.. The interior leaves a lot to be desired. I walked in into the bar area where a bored greeter was leaning and drinking something from a large glass with straws. She ignored my puzzled look. I was puzzled not by her, but by the big open space where i had expected tables to be. It looked like a dance floor or perhaps a band stand. The tables were a fair ways from where i stood looking at the stainless steel bar and the shoddy knotty pine shelving. Since no one came to greet me and seat me i sat at the bar and asked for a menu. The bartender was a pleasant enough young kid, really, too casually dressed for my tastes, but somewhat talkative. I ordered bruschetta for starters then papardelle and a spinach salad. The bruschetta were ok. It's hard to mess up toasted crunchy bread smeared with a reasonably tasty caponata. At least they were tasty. The papardelle on the other hand were not. The plate arrived looking like a foto from Saveur magazine. I was impressed until i took my first taste. The dish had been advertised as a Neapolitan ragu with pork belly. It had some pork and some oiliness that would indicate pork belly, but ragu it was not. It was a bland tomato sauce which had been slightly undercooked with smallish slices of meat added to it. Tastless, with hints of tomato. The noodles were another bland lowpoint. Slightly mushy to the bite with a floury uncooked taste which is weird because they were overcooked, way past al dente. The salad arrived suffering from the same bland malaise. Then came the desssert, a flan which was excxellent. I told the bartender that i thought it was the best thing of my meal.heI then asked what i thought of what i had eaten so I told him. Too his credit he didn't get defensive when i described it as the-chef-isn't-in-the-kitchen-country-club food. He halfway agreed and told me that they needed to hear criticism like that so they can get their direction. I hope they do. For what it all cost i expected much more in the way of an experienced restauranteur with his act already together opening a second eatery. Big let down. I do hope they pull it together, though. I believe their intentions are well placed. I can't be too optimistic however because this town is full of second rate places strutting about as if they were king of the roost.

text: This restaurant is located within the small Marriott Hotel situated on the corner of 28 Street and Roosevelt Boulevard in St. Petersburg across from the Carillon Center. I was invited to a business lunch at this location on a Wednesday at 11:30 AM. As I arrived I noticed that there is a special side door next to the pool designated as the entrance to this establishment. Entering that door into a semi-divided room separated by sheer curtain into what must be a "meeting room" with a larger table that sat 10. I took a seat at a large glass table to the left that sat 8 and waited for the vendor representative to show. There are hues of red and dark wood throughout this establishment providing a trendy upscale look. The table settings include a salad fork and a water glass keeping with the theme. There is a sign at the host station that says please see yourself we sat at a deuce that had very comfortable chairs. The service area of this particular table was nice and felt a little larger than your traditional deuce. We were quickly greeted by our server who was dressed up for Halloween in a sort of scary hockey/jeans T-shirt kind of costume, it was not really becoming at all. She informed us of the drinks selections which included un-sweet tea and Pepsi products. We both chose un-sweet tea. The menu was presented in a nice leather bound case and was simplistic enough for lunch, containing appetizers, salads, sandwiches and four entrées, Gordon Ramsay would've approved. She brought back our drinks and took our order. I ordered the Fettuccine Bolognese, and the vendor ordered the Classic Turkey Club with a house salad. Our server brought out the salads first, with both of us ordering the house dressing which was balsamic vinaigrette. A decent sized salad, that consisted of mixed greens, onions, two not so ripe olive tomatoes, and cucumbers. The dressing was decent and appropriately proportioned to the salad. The green selection was nice and the onions and cucumbers were crisp and fresh but I really couldn't get past the tomatoes. I mean I ate them mind you, but they weren't very good. Halfway through the salads we were brought out our entrées so based on that I'd have to say the timing wasn't great but we were the only table in there and perhaps the chef had not gotten into the groove yet. My pasta was served in a huge white bowl that had a very unique shape, but my first impression was that the portion seemed incredibly small. After diving in I realized that the bowl was just immense. The first impression of the turkey club was that it, like the bowl, was also quite large. The ingredients on the club were fresh and crisp, including the bread, which was wheat. It had a generous portion of turkey piled thick within. My pasta had an adequate supply of meat, with noticeable pieces of beef and pork I did not however taste any ground chicken as listed on the menu unless they make the meatballs with it. The red sauce was tasty, tangy and appropriately proportioned to the pasta. I asked for Parmesan and was brought freshly grated Parmesan which melted into this hot dish wonderfully. Two other things stuck out in my mind in regards to service. First, it seemed quite a long time before our server actually checked on us after serving the entrées. Second, when she brought the bill she announced it in the middle of our conversation. Having served tables myself, and witnessed this from other servers, the practice itself irritates me. Interrupting a conversation is inexcusable, and I don't need for you to announce the fact that you've just deposited the bill on the table. I'm pretty sure I can figure that out on my own. As for price, the Fettuccine Bolognese rings in at $10 with a house salad included and the Classic Turkey Club comes in at $8 also with a house salad or fries if you choose. I find these prices to be right on par with any sit-down establishment for lunch. Glancing at the menu, the only price changes I might make would be to reduce the pricing or portion sizes in the salad category. A fresco salad is listed as $9 and you can add chicken for $2, shrimp for $3 or ahi tuna for $5 which for a salad is pretty darned expensive. I assume the portion size would make up for it, based on the two entrées we received, however, lowering the price and the portion size would place it on par with expectations. As for our entrées, the portion sizes were really quite generous for the amount of money. I was unable to finish my salad or my entrée leaving at least five or so bites on each. The only negative in regards to product unfortunately, was that my second glass of tea was really pretty muddy and I had to ask for it. All in all price, and portion sizes, plus decent decor make this a good place for lunch. Not perfect as you will see reflected in the rating, but slightly above average. With a few minor tweaks in service and pricing or portions, and some quality control in regards to their tea, this place could be stellar.

text: Z'otz, I miss you. The old Z'otz was attached to a laundromat right off Frenchmen street. In 2003-4, when I was living in the youth hostel and managing bands, it was open 24 hours, so I'd always go there to guzzle some caffeine/eat a cookie after the music stopped. I admit, I didn't go for the coffee. I mostly went because, there was this girl who worked there. Heidi. She ran this tiny little publishing outfit, that was in some complex and probably illegal (this IS New Orleans, after all) way connected to the organizers of the Dragon's Den open-mic poetry night. She published one of my poems in a chapbook of the event. Not the good one that I sent her, but the stupid one that I don't even know how she got hold of, that was about not getting any action. She also talked me (basically by smiling) into writing joke-gothic christmas carols. She used to be an astrophysics major at Tulane, until they shut down the program, then she dropped out. Or, so she said. I suspect she made up some parts of her personal history. She also ran the publishing company under an assumed name. And she had a boyfriend. Of COURSE she had a boyfriend. They always have boyfriends. And this was that stage in my life before that fact became less of a problem. So I spent a lot of time at Z'otz. Still, it's my Z'otz. Even though now it's moved away from the music scene crowd (except, of course, for Rebirth at the Maple Leaf) way over to the Garden District and the college crowd (zzzz), and even though it's not 24 hours anymore, and even though Heidi mysteriously disappeared about the same time I did (they ALWAYS mysteriously disappear, the really hot ones, don't they? mainly because a propensity to mysteriously disappear is a main criterion for hotness, I suppose) the last time I was in town I still rode the streetcar over for the pilgrimage to my place for caffeine and cookies and unrequited lust. And I miss it.

text: I went to Revolucion for a friend's birthday party. I had already had carnitas to eat earlier on, so I didn't eat then. I did notice, however, that there were "frites" on the menu. This threw me off. Was this an attempt to be fashionable? Frites (short, pommes frites or even pommes de terre frites - Yes, I took French in High School. I don't remember much) it's French. This restaurant is *mostly* Mexican themed. Revolucion is decorated in Dia de los Meurtos (awesome!). It's really cool. There's a somewhat tiki inspiration inside, too. As soon as I sat at the table where we were (luckily there was one spare table and chair nearby to grab and pull up), I sat for awhile before realizing that the bartenders walking out to tables were only bringing food and not just ignoring me. I asked one of my friends if we had to go to the bar to order drinks. With confirmation, it was also suggested that I get two because I might be up there for awhile. It did take awhile to get a drink (I opted for a margarita- as did everyone else, it seemed). So I asked for two. It took quite awhile for the bartender to make. I know they take a bit longer than a two part cocktail, but for as long as it took to be asked what I'd like, I had two bartenders ask if I had been helped after I placed my order. I didn't have to wait quite as long each time I went to the bar after the first time. I'm glad I ordered two margaritas, though. I didn't realize until much later in the evening that there was a tiki bar in the back. Many of my friends that I was there with had left. And I had seen several people seem to "leave and come back," or so it seemed. I asked a friend, and he said he was in the Tiki bar. He showed me where it was. So I went out back, and there it was. After too many margaritas, I had already switched to captain and cokes earlier on, so maybe I needed something smooth- Something rummy for what was to come. The tiki bar was really really cool. But it also threw me off a bit. Tiki bars and tiki culture is Polynesian, not Mexican. Maybe there's a connection that I just don't know, and I'll admit that I don't know a whole lot, but I think I know a little. And it's okay to combine the two into one place. Hell, some of my favorite places have no "theme" and are so out of sorts, but they might be totally tacky, and that's sort of why I love them so much. I really liked Revolucion for it's Day of the Dead Mexican theme. Although I hadn't had the tacos yet (and plan to next time), they smelled delicious! The concept for both areas are really totally awesome. I just hope that the potential for each of them isn't squashed by the limit placed by the other. text: Like many other travelers who have used the Hertz service out of TPA, I booked my flight and rental car on Priceline about a week before my trip to Tampa and had anticipated no problems with the transaction before hand. However, after arriving at the Hertz counter, things started to go down hill quick. First, I am a member of their Gold club, and being so I proceeded straight to the garage to pick up my car. Upon arriving at that counter, I was told that because I booked on Priceline I had to go and wait with all of the other customers. Although unhappy, I understood, and did as I was told. Once inside the rental building, I noticed that all three of their self service machines were out of order. In addition, the line was literally going all the way out the door into the hot Florida sun and none of the Hertz employees seemed enthused to be there or showed any effort at getting through the line in a timely manner. Once at the counter, I handed the woman working my information and she found my reservation within seconds. "Finally!", I thought. Wrong. After looking up my information she spent about five to ten minutes trying to up sell me on upgrading from the compact car I had reserved to mid sizes, full sizes, SUVs, convertibles, you name it. After telling her numerous times, quite politely, that I was not interested, she finally leveled with me and told me they did not have the card available that I had reserved and already paid for. She then began to tell me she could give me one of the upgrades at a discounted price. After telling her once again, that I had paid for this car a week ago and made a reservation for the exact time I was there, and I did not want an upgrade, she told me I could be put on a waiting list, but she couldn't tell me how long it would be. Minutes? Hours? Days? Nothing. I can't help but wonder how she couldn't use her computer to look it up, considering everyone who rents a car has a time that they are supposed to return it at. After continuing to argue with her for a few more minutes, I told her that I would take the upgrade but I did not want to be charged for it as it was not my fault that they had not done their job in a competent manner. The woman the proceeded to tell me that because I booked my rental on Priceline, I had reserved the price and not the car and that they didn't have to hold the car for me. Of course, I told her that by that logic that I shouldn't be charged an extra fee for an upgrade anyways, as I had already reserved the price. No go. She stared at me like I was some sort of idiot. Getting tired of running in circles, and having people waiting on me, I finally took the upgrade and had to pay extra money out of my pocket for something that wasn't even my fault. I ended up driving a full size boat of a car around Tampa that I was not even comfortable driving, that hadn't even been properly cleaned (there was still dirt on the floor!), and best of all I had to pay for that wonderful upgrade. I was treated like dirt during my visit, and I left feeling lied to and unappreciated as a customer. I will NEVER use Hertz to rent a car again. If I could give the Hertz TPA location 0 stars and have it show up on Yelp, I would. Long story short: DO NOT GIVE THESE SCAM ARTISTS YOUR MONEY.

text: When I had a craving for the apparently elusive "dirty" style chicken wings, a friend of mine told me I should try Kicker's. I was starving when I finally got there and of course disappointed when I didn't see the wings I craved. Nevertheless, the waitress who doubled as the bartender was very friendly, and the place was somewhat quiet. The menu had lots of great stuff and I noticed the prices weren't very expensive so my first thought was "this can't be good food". The waitress told me the special of the 12" pizza and said that since they take a while since they are made to order, I might want to order an appetizer. I opted for the toasted ravioli. After what seemed a while and what started to bother me since my stomach was growling, the waitress came out to say they were out of the ravs since they were busy over the weekend. Ok, Potato skins would do. About 15 minutes later, the waitress came out with a plate of the biggest most loaded with cheese and bacon potato skins I've ever had experienced! Provel, chedder and strips of crispy bacon all on what I believe was half a potato that still had meat on it rather than the run of the mill potato skin that is skinny and has a blob of cheese and maybe a few sprinkles of artificial bacon if your lucky. After about 2 and a half of these, I had to stop until my pizza arrived which just as I sat back to rest, here it came. I ordered a sausage and bacon and that's exactly what it had in abundance! The sauce was in my opinion just icing on the cake of a pizza that had big chunks of sausage, not the little balled up kind, and strips of bacon that was crisp and not just there, and a layer of provel cheese that was just a little burnt on top which was just fine with me. It had to weigh at least 5 pounds! And the thickness was almost comparable to a stuffed pizza. Three pieces later, and in need of a wheel chair to leave, I asked for the check which I couldn't believe for the drinks, pizza and skins was surprising! For this quality of food I could have easily expected a $40.00 bill even with just two items and drinks. The food was amazing and I will definitely be back. There are only 3 benches in the whole locker room. This is for a gym with hundreds of active members. Often no where to sit down or unpack your gym bag. If you like to go to the gym before work and expect to shower/shave there, forget it. The sinks are ridiculous. They have pressure valves where the water barely trickles out and its all cold. Shaving or brushing your teeth is impossible. The water pressure in the showers is not much better and there is no where to hang your towel or place your soap or shampoo. Even worse, the showers face the crappers so you are surrounded by a real nice aroma while you are trying to get clean. They have a sauna but its never hot. What's worse is the culture at this gym is to go into the sauna fully clothed with shoes on. Guys prop their dirty shoes (I've even seen workboots) up on the benches. This is no spa-like sauna. Stay out if you're used to using saunas properly. Juice bar? They have one but its expensive and you'll be lucky if its open when you need it. It seems to be closed Friday nights and all weekend. Bottom line: come in your gym clothes, work out, and leave. Keep low expectations.

text: This is a hidden gem (if you are Brazilian or enjoy Brazilian food). When you come in, you are most likely going to be greeted in Portuguese. If you don't feel like having a Brazilian style lunch, they also serve sandwiches and burgers, Brazilian style snacks like empanadas, coxinhas, pasteis (you probably don't know what they are... but trust me, they are delicious). text: Purchased a groupon with several friends to go to a Belgian beer pairing with a 5 course meal here recently. I will start by saying I am a huge beer enthusiast and know a fair amount on the subject, but I have never been to a dinner like this so I was looking forward to an evening of fun and learning. The night started with a self-guided tour of the house. If you like old historic houses this will definitely be right up your alley. It is a beautiful old home and has a very nice design, some of the modern updates do hurt the look and feel of the building though. Unfortunately this was the nicest part of the evening. After taking the tour we return to the downstairs for a beer reception. The reception consisted of about ten different beers being opened and approximately 2 ounces poured each time you passed through the line. MAYBE 1/3 of these beers were Belgian, the staff had no information or opinion on them, and they were served in whatever order they were grabbed which made tasting difficult as no water or bread was provided and going from a double chocolate stout to a blonde ruins your palette. The tasting line wound through the old house with no order, huge bottlenecks, and was served by a staff with no personality or sense of humor. After spending an hour standing to receive approximately 10 ounces of beer we were called to sit in the dining room and given a run down of the history of the house and encouraged to come to a wine pairing class. We were then told by owner Karen Glass that she didn't care for beer because it tasted terrible and their dinner was thrown together(which showed). The first course comes out and consisted of a piece of bread with cheese on it and was paired with blonde. So far so good, but unfortunately this was the best part of the meal. The beers were served in 2 ounce pours while anybody that requested wine got full pours into a bottomless glass. From the beginning they made it apparent they favored wine and even at a BEER dinner we would still be treated as second class. The second course comes out and it's a brown rice mixed with salad and vinaigrette(was someone drunk in the kitchen?) It was a horrible combination of blandness paired with a cherry ale(the ale was delicious, but again 2 ounces and you're cut off). Time for course three, muscles. The muscles were flavored well, but were served colder than my room temperature salad rice mixture and paired with more of the cherry ale(at least with a second 2 ounce pour I got to try a little more). At this point we discuss leaving, but thanks to terrific company at our table we decided to make the most of it and to stick it out. The fourth course comes out and it includes an overcooked pot roast mush mixed with salad(Really more salad?) and a shot of doppelbock. At this point we try requesting more beers and we're informed that there was wine available if we wanted something else to drink. (Thanks, I thought I paid for a BEER dinner.) And we move on to the fifth and final course of the night(Thank goodness, I can't wait to go get a pint and something that resembles food). Karen informs us that she would have liked to have served waffles(obviously this is the extent of her knowledge when it comes to Belgian food) but instead decided on an overcooked and rock hard butter cake that was no doubt left over from one of her MUCH more sophisticated wine dinners that none of us simpletons would appreciate. It was paired with a shot of raspberry lambic and we were promptly given our checks for taxes and gratuity. In summary this may be a nice place for a wine dinner(or a beer dinner where you'd rather have wine) and you don't care about the quality of food or the friendliness of the staff. For what I paid I could have had a fantastic dinner at any number of restaurants in Indy and spoken with a much more informed waiter regarding my choices in beer without having judgement passed on me. Steer clear unless you enjoy disappointment.
label: NEG

text: FRIED CHICKEN! LAMB BURGERS! Do I have your attention? Last night my husband and I ate at North Third and even though the decor was a combination of trendy and frightening, the food was nothing short of awesome. We ordered the pierogies as an appetizer. They came out smothered in sour cream and onions, and while they had a little bit of browning on them, it wasn't so much that they felt chewy, burnt, or crunchy. Definitely a good start to the meal. For my meal I ordered the fried chicken, mashed potatoes, jalepeno cornbread, and cole slaw special. The fried chicken was really good - I'm confident that there was honey on it, which made it just a little bit sweet. The mashed potatoes were so smooth they should have been called whipped/beaten/pulverized potatoes. The jalepeno cornbread was a little spicy but, like the chicken, also a little bit sweet. The texture was perfect - not dry at all. I even ate some of the cole slaw, and I am not a cole slaw fan (I hate the creaminess/thickness of it). My husband got the lamb burger with feta and arugula. The lamb itself was medium-rare and the portion was pretty large. The amount of feta on this thing was obscene, and the bread that held it all together was perfectly soft but supportive. It came with a side of fries that were well seasoned and he ordered a side of brussel sprouts also, which we both enjoyed. What I wasn't really a fan of were the cocktails. I started with the blood orange margarita and it was only OK. I've been eating at a lot of Mexican joints lately and this margarita didn't stand up to some others I've had. I then went with the "Stoli Doli." WHOA!! That thing was straight up liquor with like a teaspoon of pineapple juice. I couldn't finish it because it was just way too strong. Overall the food here was spectacular. There wasn't one thing I ate that I didn't like. I certainly would return!

text: The reputation & Yelp reviews led me to choose Bouchon for my birthday dinner. Wow, what a disappointment! We (party of 2) arrived at our reservation time of 8:30pm. The hostess initially sat us at a beautiful 4-top on the patio, close to the entrance, and with plenty of space to relax. About 2 minutes later she came back and said she'd made a mistake, and that she needed the table for a party of four. In reality, a 2-top had just opened up (the table still need to be cleaned). We politely agreed to be moved, but ended up being squeezed into a very tight corner of the patio. No apology. No offer of a round of drinks on-the-house for freeing up the larger table for them. Nothing. Our waiter was nice, but paid much more attention to the four local women at the table next to us. When we ordered, he didn't bother to give us much detail on the dishes. The four women got detailed descriptions. We also asked for the wine steward, so he could recommend good pairings. What we got was another waiter who served wine. The four women got the Sommelier, even though they brought their own bottle of wine. The appetizers were OK at best. Heirloom tomato salad, and pork belly (although the waiter that served literally called it BACON!). For the main course, I had the chicken over risotto. I was shocked when I took my first bite -- the chicken tasted like salted cardboard. That's how dry it was. It must have been forgotten in the oven, or left under a heat lamp. It was not edible, though I will give them credit that the risotto was good (but not great). When I told the waiter, he was nice enough to offer to replace the dish with a fresh one, or exchange for a new dish. I opted to switch to the white fish. When that finally arrived (and by that time my partner was done with his dish), it too was overcooked. My partner had ordered the duck, which is a signature dish for the restaurant. He said that the breast was quite rare, but the rest was overlooked. Even one of the women at the table next to us had to send her duck back, because she "preferred to eat it cooked." Moving onto to desert, we decided to share the Molten Lava cake. This was actually the best tasting dish we had all night, so hats-off the the desert chef! To accompany desert, I ordered a coffee, which was really mediocre for a 5-star restaurant. It tasted like standard drip coffee without much boldness or flavor. But worse than that, when my partner ordered chamomile tea, the waiter brought a little teapot of hot water and an empty cup with a Tazo tea bag (still in the wrapper) sitting in it! Really?? This is the best they could do??? All during the meal, we had an assortment of empty glasses stacking up on the table. Even though the waiter, busboy, and wine-waiter had all been by our table several times throughout the night, not one bothered to clear an empty glass. We literally had to ask them to do it. To cap off a really below-average birthday dinner, they didn't even put a candle on the desert, when the reservation clearly listed it was a birthday. And to make matters even worse, when the waiter presented the check, he apologized for the overcooked chicken, and said that he had asked the manager to remove it from the check. However, when my partner looked at the check, we were still being charged for both the chicken & the fish entrees. We had to point this out to the waiter on the check, because he clearly had not reviewed it himself. And when we did, he removed it from the check himself, no manager involved. Overall, a huge disappointment. And based on my experience, I would certainly not recommend this restaurant to anyone.

Also they charge you for 7 or more pieces left on the table, so just don't be a fatso and order a few pieces at a time and sit back and let the happiness come! So basically if you want to impress a date and do it on the kind of cheap while also demonstrating your ability to eat so much that your head nearly explodes than this is the perfect place! text: I admit it... I'm a sucker for restaurants that have been on TV. I don't care what TV show its on, if I've heard the restaurant sucks, if its not the type of food that I'm into.. if a restaurant is featured on television, you can bet your bottom dollar that I'm going to get my tush there at some point. Morimoto's Toro Tartare was featured on Food Network's "Best Thing I Ever Ate". My homeboy, Duff Goldman, raved about this dish. Full disclosure: He was at the NYC location, but I care to overlook that. It's not like I'd have money for the train after this meal anyway. Recently, my husband and I headed over to celebrate my birth. We were bound and determined to try the toro tartare. We contemplated doing the omakase menus, but after learning the toro tartare is only included in the $120 pp menu, we decided against it. Because a) we are cheap and b) last time I did a tasting menu I had to unzip my dress in the car. Now we didn't have our elastic pants on nor did we bring our bars of gold, so we decided to just order a few things off the menu. Here is what we tried: Toro Tartare: Awesome presentation, but I felt like it didn't live up to the hype (Sorry, Duff-ster). Definitely delicious but at $26 it didn't grab me Seared scallop: AWESOME. Portion came with two scallops, topped with shittake mushrooms, grilled corn, bacon, and a creamy corn sauce. I wanted to lick the plate. Vegetable tempura roll: Loved this dish as well. I loved the crunch of the tempura with the soft, almost creaminess of the sweet potato. Yum! Lobster Ceviche Salad: I got this as my main course. What might look like a tiny hole in the wall in Northeast Philly is probably one of the greatest family-owned Jewish bakeries out there. People say that your sense of smell is your most evocative sense, and they're right. I was immediately thrust back in time at least fifteen years when that wave of sweetness hit my nostrils. The knishes are easily one of the best things they make. My favorites are by far the rice and the pizza knishes. Remember to toast it up before you eat it for optimum flavor potential (do NOT microwave their knishes)! Give it time to cool down, so you don't burn your tongue, but once it's cool enough to touch, toss the silverware aside and go all fingers with it. You'll abandon the fork and knife anyway as soon as you taste it. They also make a mean cheesecake, and the rest of their desserts are great too. Try their baklava and really anything with sugar on it. Nothing's too moist or too dry here - everything is just the way it should be. You can't beat the prices either. I plan on going back the next time I'm in town for another nostalgic experience of pure Jewish deliciousness. And I can't wait!

text: Traveling through the small towns surrounding Philadelphia can certainly be an adventure. From winding roads to suddenly changing names of streets, the actual journey alone can be exciting. Valentino's is similar to many of the Italian style restaurants that dot the suburban Philadelphia countryside. I am always amazed at how many "Pizza" and "Italian" restaurants there are in the seemingly middle of nowhere. Most of them are located in strip malls and seldom seem to have any differentiating qualities. The restaurant is certainly pleasant, the owners and the staff are gracious and very warm. I actually stopped in after looking at a few other restaurants and Valentino's was the only one with any customers inside. It was a normal dinner time, and seeing as how Valentino's had a crowd I thought it was a promising sign. Although I enjoyed the service and appreciated finding a lively restaurant rather than an eerily quiet one to eat in I cannot say that I overwhelmingly enjoyed the food. The portions are generous and several of the dishes are presented in a home cooking style. However, there is little balance applied to the seasonings, with some being too bland and some being too salty or bitter. Several of the pasta dishes were overcooked to the point where the pasta broke apart on the tongue. If you have problems with your teeth this could be a positive thing. I certainly got the opinion that Valentino's is a popular locals destination. I believe they try hard. However, it was very hard for me to leave this place feeling satisfied especially when the bill came to more than $20 per person.

text: First impression upon walking in is that the place is huge and they have more TV's than you have ever seen. Not a bad thing. Then you try to speak with a hostess to get a table and EVENTUALLY they will acknowledge you but then on my first visit for Monday Night Football I was told that no tables were available. Okay, that seemed a bit strange given that I saw at least 5-10 four tops that were completely open and only a couple people who appeared to be waiting for tables by the host station but instead we chose to sit at the bar, have a few drinks, and some appetizers. Even at the bar service was fairly slow but they made an okay drink and finally the food came out after quite a long wait. Cochon de Lait tacos were actually quite good - after adding salt. The side dish of Mac & Cheese was also decent - after adding salt. The space has huge ceilings and lots of wood and TV's as you would expect from an upscale sports bar, plus the outside courtyard including bar seats that are served through open windows is a pretty cool option. There only appeared to be one large TV outside though so for watching games it's probably not ideal. In terms of food it appears Manning's does a decent job for a sports bar other than the kitchen having an aversion to salt so only eat here if you're comfortable adding salt to bring out the flavor in whatever you order. On my first vist Manning's was average or maybe a bit below - it's obviously got a ton of Harrah's money in it so I don't really call this a "locally owned" place despite Archie Manning's involvement. I'd like to go with 2.5 stars (which Yelp reviews appear to have pegged perfectly) but will round down to 2 and I definitely prefer to spend my money at local places in the future. However, with the lack of good sports bars in NOLA where you can get a seat and have decent food I may return to Manning's at some point. I'd like to hope it will be better, but all around there is little indication that much improvement can be expected.
label: NEG

text: This has to be the nastiest airport this side of Port-Au-Prince. A few of the highlights of my trip there: - The whole place was under construction while I was there, and based on the other reviews, this seems to be an ongoing thing. - The TSA was one of the worst I'd ever encountered. Think of a "security checkpoint" run by ghetto refuse that looks like it was hired straight out of a halfway house in the dangerous part of New Orleans that they tell you to avoid. Expect to spend 45 minutes in line for the privilege of being barked at by angry and illiterate agents whose only skill seems to be to push a button that makes the conveyer belt go forward...and push your unattended luggage off the end of the table while you wait for them to wave you into the scanner. - There was only one single restaurant on the other side of security that was open. They had a couple others "under construction" supposedly, though no sign of being anywhere near completion. It was packed with hungry travelers and no seating room. - That one restaurant was out of everything. I ordered a beer. They were out of the first two types I requested. I ordered chicken. They were out of chicken. I ordered a roast beef sandwich. They were out of beef. I ordered a cajun shrimp gumbo dish. They were out of shrimp. So I stood up and walked out. - The snack options aren't any better and way overpriced - e.g. $4 for a drink, $2.50 for a regular sized candybar, and poor selections. - Nobody who works there seems to have a clue what they're doing. I asked a random worker there where the freaking restroom was (it ended up being obscured behind some construction barrier). He shrugged and mumbled he didn't know. This happened multiple times when I asked for directions to different things in the airport. Oh and one final warning - DO NOT take the airport shuttle thing to downtown. It is overpriced and sloooooowwww. I have never been on a slower shuttle in my life. It wasn't because of traffic, but because they take this convoluted route to all the downtown hotels and try to cram as many different passengers as they can into each shuttle, all of them going to different places. The result? If you're lucky you get the first stop, but more likely than not you'll be driving in circles a few blocks from your hotel for half an hour before they finally get to it. I was in direct sight of my hotel 3 different times before I finally asked the driver if I could just get out and walk from the next stop. The return shuttle wasn't any better - they scheduled the pickup about 4 hours before my flight left, then I literally road around downtown in circles for an hour while the driver "passed time" while waiting for other hotel pickups to be radioed in until the entire shuttle was full. It was only a 20 min drive from there to the hotel once we actually left downtown, which meant I got to the airport 2.5 hours ahead of my flight and had to sit there in the world's nastiest terminal. Seriously - if you can avoid this place, do it. Fly into Baton Rouge or Gulfport, rent a car, and drive yourself to New Orleans instead of going through this awful, inefficient dumpster of an airport.
label: NEG

text: I don't know if there are words in English to explain how amazing Minado is, but I'm going to try my best. My first trip to Minado was about three years ago. I went again this summer, and the magic is still alive. Let's break this down a little: the main draw of the place is the sushi. They have every type of sushi that you could want, and some you never even knew you wanted (until you try them, that is). The sushi alone covers one long side of the sushi bar (3-sided). The sushi is presented on huge plates, with maybe 50 individual pieces when filled. There is a team of sushi chefs behind the bar, making fresh rolls to replace the ones that are taken. On the next side of the bar is the sashimi, which is also amazing. The third side of the bar has many types of exotic salads, for lack of a better term. There are carrot salads, mushroom salads, octopus salads- again, anything you could want. Now, just that alone would be enough to get me to Minado. But wait! There's more! There's a long table that has all kinds of fried and tempura foods. Another tables holds kebabs, dumplings, soups, and other hot deliciousness. There is a man at the hot grill thing that will cook your food (meats, noodles, etc) however you ask. Then, to end this beautiful experience, there is a dessert table. The desserts are mini, so I don't feeling guilty grabbing one of everything. The best part of the dessert is, of course, the ice cream machine, for two reasons. One, I spent a summer working at Rita's, so I can make a mean ice cream swirl/spiral, and I like showing off. Two, GREEN TEA ICE CREAM. No further questions, your honor.

text: I wanted to write about my disappointment about a change Max Brenner made on their chocolate pizza in the Philadelphia restaurant. A few years ago, I came to this restaurant and tried the most amazing chocolate pizza. The crust played an important role in this delectable dessert. It was really "The Best Thing I Ever Ate"-worthy. However, somewhere along the line, someone decided to change the recipe. It now tastes like they got lazy and use a store-bought pizza crust and slapped some chocolate and marshmallows on top. I went back several times in hope that it was just a fluke, however, each time thereafter, I was continually disappointed. Most of the time it came out burnt and dry. What a waste of calories and money. Such a disappointment. I really wished they didn't mess with a masterpiece by changing the recipe. The original chocolate pizza was chewy and delicious. The new pizza is hard and dry. It's not worth getting. I could make my own chocolate pizza, using store-bought pizza DOUGH, Nutella, etc., and it would blow this pizza out of the water. Save your money. I found their other desserts to be eh...leaving much to be desired. They are often overly sweet leaving me feeling nothing but really thirsty - literally for water, and metaphorically desiring something to satisfy my sweet tooth. There is more to a dessert than being just sweet (or overly sweet). There needs to be a balance. Sometimes I found their ingredients to be stale. If I am going to spend as much money as it costs to eat here (way overpriced for the quality they provide by the way), it better be worth it. I don't mind spending a lot of money on food because to me, (delicious) food is one of life's luxuries. You'll find that I would be willing to spend, and have spent up to $100 on a meal - and I didn't mind because the food was exquisite. HOWEVER, I do NOT feel like my money is well spent at Max Brenner. I feel like it is one of those restaurants that I could tell people to try just because of the idea of the restaurant (huge dessert menu), but I wouldn't recommend it as a place I would visit again. Especially since I've come back numerous times myself in hopes of getting better desserts, only to be disappointed. Again, they have a such a great idea with a restaurant that focuses a lot on dessert because I feel like this is something the city lack. A place to go to enjoy varieties of desserts. When you look at the menu, there are brilliant ideas. However, they fail in execution. The chocolate is exquisite, but their other ingredients lack quality; therefore, the entire dessert only serves to disappoint. Each bite does not make me yearn for more. Each bite I take, I am hoping it'll taste better but it never does. I hope the restaurant takes these criticisms and improve. I only take time out of my day to write about these criticisms because I would like to see the restaurant improve. Like I previously said over and over, they have a great idea for the restaurant, but they need to make the finished product (the actual dessert) as amazing as the descriptions provided in their menu. I want to see them succeed mainly because I want a place to go, socialize, and enjoy AMAZING desserts!

text: La Vallesana is a special place. The kind of place that you go significantly out of your way to revisit. The kind of place whose tacos you crave again the moment you're done digesting your first basketful. The kind of place whose name you can't wait to drop into a conversation with friends, accompanied by a confident recommendation and a subtle hint at your own worldliness. And it's not just because their menu features the words "cow tongue." I have made it a personal quest of mine to visit as many of our fine county's Mexican restaurants as I possibly can. My current tally is in the hundreds (it's a quest, folks). And I can proudly say that La Vallesana is one of my top 5 favorite places nationwide. The one menu item that really elevates this place into the upper echelon... AL PASTOR. If you've never tried Al Pastor, it is chopped pork that has been marinated and slow-cooked with pineapple, which gives the meat a hint of sweetness and helps break it down until it is off-the-charts tender and juicy. The Al Pastor tacos at La Vallesana are the best of their kind that I have ever had the pleasure of tasting. If you've never experienced the joys of great Al Pastor, this is the place to take the leap. Trust me. You can start to get an idea of La Vallesana's greatness from some video footage of their original location and their chicken tacos in my tour webisode here: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ctZHxwRsBZU The above video was captured during my very first visit to La Vallesana. My friend Charlie and I had been driving all day from Michigan and we hadn't been to St Louis before, so we literally pulled off the highway, stopped into Benton Park Coffee, and Yelped for the nearest Mexican. And by the great grace of Montezuma, our search led us to this glorious mecca of Mexican food authenticity. Since my first visit, I have been able to return to La Vallesana, through more divine providence, dozens of times. Everything my friends and I have had there has been excellent. The tacos (priced at $1.75 each) have been my go-to items. Beside the Al Pastor, their chicken, chorizo (ground Mexican sausage), and Adobada (spicy pork) have always treated me well. Note: the chicken and chorizo tacos must be ordered two at a time, so be prepared for that. In conclusion, La Vallesana is a gem. If you are in St Louis, you do not want to pass up this opportunity for an unforgettable taco experience.
