text: I recently purchased a blighted property with my siblings in Mid-City. We are historically renovating the property. We began plumbing the building and planned on replacing the existing water meter, which has not been updated since the house was originally built in 1910, with two new meters and new pipes that funnel to our water meters. I spoke to the House Connections department in SWBNO and she quoted the installation cost between $1,800 and $2,500. She explained that sometimes an installation can cost upwards of $5,000 for a meter installation, but we would only have to pay $2,500 at the most. I received the estimate ten days later: $5,068.20. This was only for one meter and we would have to pay the whole amount. When I tried to understand why it was so drastically different from the other prices I was given, they explained that it is never the SWBNO's policy to give clients average price estimates, even though two of her employees already had, and she referred me to master of maintenance. The master of maintenance had very little insight as to how the water meter installation prices were actually determined. He said this was the SWBNO's primary contractor's domain: Fleming Construction. He said Fleming Construction set the prices and SWBNO followed suit. He tried to help to the best of his ability, but the reality was that he merely managed SWBNO's contract with Fleming. I called Jefferson Parish's water board to see how much they charged for installing a one-inch water meter. They charge a flat rate of $1,500. The city pays for the pipes on public property and the homeowner pays for the portion within their property line. I discovered that most municipalities across America operate in the same fashion (Chicago, Illinois, Tucson, Arizona), and some counties go as far as incur all of the costs for new meter installation, because they regard it as standard updating and maintenance of infrastructure. Other city's water utilities provide thorough pricing schedules for different types of water meter installation scenarios. The pricing reasoning is well documented and fully accessible to the customer. This creates a predictable and fair planning environment. SWBNO's policy of expecting homeowners to foot the entire bill for maintenance and updates that should have already occurred stands in direct opposition to Mayor Landrieu and the City Council's goal of fighting blight, fixing the condition of our deteriorating streets, and minimizing city operating costs. Investors require a predictable and transparent city government. Most investors can absorb a certain amount of variable costs, but I doubt that after someone has purchased a home, and then secured a construction loan like we have, that they will be liquid enough to pay a little over $10,000 to partially subsidize a municipal service that should have been maintained. As a historic district, most of the Mid-City housing stock boasts water meters from when the neighborhood was initially drained in the 1910's. We later discovered that our existing meter was made of toxic lead. If we ever hope to address the chronic blight that has pre-dated 2005, then we must not penalize would-be investors by forcing them to pay for the mistakes of a mismanaged bureaucracy. We must fairly and efficiently address our infrastructure while also mending the structural issues of the SWBNO that have culminated in this citywide crisis. I am not an engineer, economist, or a city planner, but since no one in the SWBNO seems to hold these credentials either, I feel equally qualified in stating that updating the pipes in such a piece-meal fashion will ultimately waste time and money for the city and Orleans Parish taxpayers. In my subsequent dealings with the SWBNO I learned that it contracts out all of their engineering, maintenance, and pavement repairs to private contractors. The employees manning their offices have no immediate access to these contracts, making it impossible for home and business owners to coordinate reasonable time schedules for repairs and updates occurring on or near their properties. As the city considers another price increase for the SWBNO's services I believe we must seriously consider what services they actually provide. Much scrutiny has been directed towards the SWBNO's Director Marcia St. Martin's salary, pension plan, and performance as a director. They are well-deserved critiques and must not be abandoned. Further inspection should also be directed toward the employees of the SWBNO. There are undoubtedly many hardworking and experienced individuals at the SWBNO, but I believe those who are none of those things outnumber them by a great majority. The Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans is not just another utility company. It is charged with working against extraordinary subsidence, functioning as a stopgap against disease spurred on by standing water, and keeping our city from drowning when it rains. We have to expect better.
label: NEG

text: I can only echo the complimentary posts below. Forget what this place looks like and go for the food. It's unbelievably good. It is obvious when you walk into Zaika that it suffers from an identity crisis. A sparsely stocked grocery meets butcher meets takeout/casual restaurant with tables. What's going on here I asked the waiter/owner during our meal? He said that they initially opened as a grocery and Halal butcher and began making some food on the side for takeout. The food started to take off surpassing the grocery sales so they scaled back on the dry goods and replaced aisles with tables. I applauded their flexibility to do whatever it takes to make it in this economy. They do, however, plan on making some updates to the space so it feels more like a proper casual dining room in the coming year. Good for them. So if you can get past the temporary aesthetics and lack of ambience you might be greatly rewarded with some fine Pakistani (very similar to Indian) food as we were. We started with crisp vegetable samosas full of peas, potato and spices with a sweet vinegar sc on the side. An excellent standard version. For mains we had Chicken Tikka Masala, Chicken Korma, Lamb sagwalla and Paneer Jalfrezi. We added 2 orders of basmati rice and 2 naans, 1 garlic and 1 house specialty with chili. I won't go into every dish but the sauces in each had long layers of balanced flavors. The meat in the chicken and lamb dishes was of very good cuts and quality. The rice was and the naans, with their soft centers and crispy edges, loaded with herbs and spices was spot on. A couple of the best naans we've had. Our 2 friends who've never eaten Indian food (but are surprisingly open to new cuisines and can handle spicy food) were dumfounded that they've never tried this food before let alone this place. I said they were being spoiled because it isn't always this good. Service was very friendly without being intrusive. They made sure we were comfortable with the spicing by providing mild/med/hot options. We went medium not knowing how they gauge. The food was spicy without setting us on fire. Nothing we couldn't handle. Except for that chili naan which made us numb but in a good way if you like spicy food. We love this place and will probably stay at the 4 Points Sheraton again just so we can revisit (when we go to Sesame Place again). I also plan on bringing a good cooler for leftovers. I was so upset to have to leave them at the hotel. Oh, and it's byo too if you like your wine and/or beer (as we do)

text: Probably one of the hippest restaurants and bars in Reno, Midtown Eats emulates places in NYC and San Francisco without living up to them in quality of the food or service. Just to be clear if you are in Reno and need a nice place with decent modern American food this is probably one the best bets. If you love hipster style and neo-vintage design and shop on Etsy this place is made for you. In a decade of eating in Reno on various yearly treks through the city, it is one of the few places I would return to. The French Spouse thinks it should get 4 stars for her food which was the soup of the day, a vegetarian mushroom soup and the tempura fried portobella mushroom burger. The fries were very good and the portobella burger was far more than just a mushroom on a bun. It was layered with cheese, sauces and veggies that gave it a complex flavour. However my Pork Belly was tough and bland and really should not have been served at all. Pork Belly isn't the easiest cut to cook and the chef here needs a refresher in cooking it. It was served with pickled cabbage and a potato gratin that also had a rather vinegary taste. We finished off with a lavender creme brulee which had a very uneven layer of sugar bruleed on top and the lavender was a bit strong. The service was very uneven, they were clearly understaffed as the host/owner was focusing mostly on a large table of his friends as well as a couple of other tables he seemed to know well and the waitress was also mixing all the cocktails. It was a weeknight but almost all the tables were full and with that many people and only two people to both mix drinks and serve there are going to be service issues. Another good thing about it being in Reno is the prices are lower that what you would find for the same dishes in LA, SF, or NYC but alas the quality also isn't as high. The entire meal was only 51 dollars including two aussie soft drinks.
label: POS

text: I've been thinking about this review for over a month now making sure that I was being fair. The food was a mixed bag for us. The fried rabbit liver with pepper jelly was beyond awesome and I nearly ordered another plate of it immediately after the first bite. The fried boudin balls were good, though I preferred the ones we had at lunch at Boucherie more. The Louisiana pork was mildly disappointing - I'd had better pulled pork many times before at 1/4 the price and our cracklins were missing the crack and were kind of flabby. My wife loves mac and cheese and all three of us really loved the pancetta-studded version at Butcher, so we figured it would be a no brainer here. Nope, as it turns out, not great. Dessert was further down the scale still. The hummingbird cake was dry and rather unpleasant. The pineapple upside-down cake was pretty unremarkable and pairing it with a lime sorbet emphasized all the wrong notes of the dulce and the pineapple. And then there was the service, which was uniformly bad. I called from the hotel to let them know that we'd be a few minutes late. "No promises," the front of house said. "Our reservations are full tonight." So we scooped up my sleeping daughter into the stroller and started running. As the time for the reservation crept closer and we hadn't yet arrived, my wife told me to run on ahead. I was glad to see lots of people out walking on Tchoupitoulas or I wouldn't have really dared. I arrived, on the verge of out of breath, to find a restaurant that wasn't half full. Now, had I called and said "we're going to be an hour late," I would get making a point of not intending to hold our reservation on a Friday night. But by the time we finished eating, the restaurant still wasn't even approaching full. I'd fully explained that I had a sleeping kid that was possibly going to make us late. Why not cut us some slack? Our server started out charming and ended up absent. He walked us through the menu and made a few recommendations, and the food got out to us in short order. When it came time to get a check, though, he disappeared for 45 minutes. My poor daughter, 30 minutes short on her nap (my fault) and having put on her party manners at some fairly upscale establishments over the past week, absolutely lost it about ten minutes into that 30 and my wife left to return to the hotel for her. I watched our server flit around the room, taking drink orders and flirting with the ladies for the rest of the 20 minutes before he returned with the ARE YOU KIDDING DID WE REALLY SPEND THAT MUCH check. I'm not one to often tip below 20%, but between the reservation static and making me wait so that he could run up people's bar tabs, I was feeling punitive. This was our last night in NOLA. Earlier in the trip, I'd almost bought a shirt at Butcher but figured, since Cochon was around the corner, that I'd return and grab it after we ate. Sadly, the Cochon experience colored Butcher enough that I left without the shirt. I'll skip Cochon next time and camp at Butcher instead for half the price and better food.

text: To preface: I had not been to Chaffin's in some 3 years, and was reluctant to return due to some negative reviews regarding a change in management. Convenience and curiosity won out and my fears about this unassuming neighborhood joint proved unfounded. The wife and I showed up around 1PM on a Sunday, and the parking lot was half empty, score. We were seated immediately and greeted by a revamped and much more accessible menu than the previous multi-page handwritten weirdness. All your favorites are there, with a variety of benedicts and burritos, as well as some novel combinations (bacons banana pancakes?) and regional delicacies like Loco Moco. The wife had her heart set on a vegetarian Benedict, but since we showed up so late on a busy sunday, they were long out of Hollandaise. We were on our way out the door when the chef himself stopped us and offered to make a new batch up fresh since the rush had died down. The California Benedict was really good with fresh ingredients and yummy hollandaise, and exactly what she needed. I opted for the country-friend steak burro as it combined all my favorite breakfast foods, and was shocked to see a wrap roughly the size of my head (and well larger than my stomach) arrive. Hash browns, egg, cheese, bacon and breaded cube steak, wrapped in a fresh tortilla and smothered in country gravy and garnished with yet another portion of chicken fried steak, this burrito is not for the faint of heart. It was delicious and everything I could ever want in a breakfast entree. BRAVO! The waitstaff was friendly and attentive, and made a fresh pot of decaf for the wife. The kitchen was lightning-fast despite the burden of making fresh Hollandaise. The ambiance is low-key with an open kitchen, vintage album covers on the wall and a back room for private rendez vous. Just over 20 dollars for two entrees, two coffees, juice and plenty of leftover burro is a great deal and the location is so convenient, right off Broadway. The only caveat is that my vegetarian wife described the hash browns as tasting "a little meaty." All in all a great meal at a great diner for a great price. 5 stars up!

text: This is the best restaurant in Edmonton. Enough said. I've been about 5 times in the last couple of years. My fiance and I used to frequent il Portico before it was suddenly shut down. As an alternative, we decided to try Wildflower across the street one night for my birthday. I LOVE this place. It's modern inside, but still has a very cozy and initmate feel. They also have a great wine and drink list, so I suggest trying a little bit of everything if you can. Ask the waiters, as they are VERY well versed in what wines pair well with what menu item, and what to suggest if you like a type of grape, but want to try something new. Every meal begins with an amuse bouche to tease the palette. Next you are served freshly baked brioche with an accompaniment of a couple of different handmade butters. I highly recommend getting a full meal (appetizer, main course, dessert), to get the full experience. I order different things every time I'm there (I've had the lamb, the chicken, and the bison tenderloin so far), and have yet to have a bad meal. My fiance always orders their salmon cakes entree, which comes with lobster, scallops, gnocchi and more. It's always amazing and never disappoints. The best part is, is you don't feel like you've eaten a ton of food. Compared to the Hardware Grill (which was good, but there was WAY too much food), this is perfectly portion controlled so you don't feel like you need to be rolled out of the restaurant.

The Thai place is wonderful too. The red curry was too much for just one meal--I ate it over two. Dinner *and* lunch for just $7!! There are SO many places here which I plan on gradually exploring over the coming months...I'll add to this if I come across anything exceptional. But if you're in Philly and haven't been there yet, GO NOW.

text: Update: 12/20/11 Previous sushi disappointment now resolved. Felt much better finding each piece quite cold, as room temp sushi doesn't inspire confidence. Lots of sushi choices, all very flavorful, now food scores a 5 on a buffet scale. Update: 10/10/11 Stopped by Oriental Super Buffet today for lunch. As another reviewer has written, OSB has undergone a huge renovation. There literally isn't a single surface in the entire restaurant that hasn't been upgraded substantially, from the ceiling/walls/floors/tables to the serving tables, a new sushi bar and hibachi grill. Even the entrance to the restaurant has been upgraded with a substantial exterior porch & woodwork and interior entrance with a huge rock waterfall flowing into a pond that has steam rising out of it. Overall the tasteful, contemporary design with historical/cultural Chinese references creates an atmosphere that's a large step above the old building and most Chinese buffets I've ever been to. As for the food, what used to be small section of a serving table of sushi choices is now a display about 30' long with 20 different items, all prepared by a full-time sushi chef that closely monitors the appearance and cleanliness. I sampled about 8 different sushi, and found about half of them good, but not great, the others average. And a good part of the reason for that was for some reason the trays of sushi, even though they sat on abundant heaps of ice, didn't keep them as cool as I like, nor as I recall they used to be. I seem to recall before they placed the sushi on on a type of china or hard white platters what would get very cold on the ice, and now I think they're on plastic trays which just get cool instead of cold. At least that's my theory. As much as I wanted to get excited about such a varied selection, it was the only disappointment of the meal. The hibachi grill was manned full-time and was very busy with orders being served up quickly. The buffet now includes fresh mussels and clams, both a nice addition the holdover of mountains of boiled peel & eat shrimp on beds of ice that I could never and still can't resist.. OSB's previous quality/quantity of fish/seafood dishes always attracted me, and the selection is better than ever. All of the old standard dishes seem to be on the line, along with a few additions, one of which was Mongolian beef that I found mildly spicy and very flavorful...probably my favorite. Other bright spots were black pepper shrimp and a crab dish that had huge chunks of crab under a layer of melted cheese. Very good. There are adequate salad and desert bars, along with a fruit bar that had large quantities of fresh kiwi that were absolutely delicious., When we didn't see the smiling owner who was always there in greeting us by name I found it a little odd. I ended up chatting with another diner who said he had passed away, and the new owner decided to immediately renovate before taking over. The new owner was a commanding presence in the way he monitored the status and cleanliness of the serving tables and attention the wait staff gave us. More than once I saw him call one of the staff working the serving tables to thoroughly clean their counters and refill steam trays of food. Under his gaze there was very little that escaped his attention, which gave me confidence about the food. The flavor and food quality is still there, and the prices are still good ($7.99 lunch/$11.99 dinner, and an additional 20% off promotion for the grand re-opening.). Even drinks are reasonably priced at $1.50. For the ~$6.50 price I paid or even $8 regularly, it's a great value. While I always loved the old OSB, it's apparent it's now in very capable hands that have set a high standard for quality and should maintain it. I've been to bigger Chinese buffets, but very few that have OSB's quality. The renovation upgrade bumps my score up a notch, and on my Pinellas Chinese buffet scale, OSB now gets 5's for atmosphere, service, and value, but the sushi disappointment dropped the food to a 4. 9/7/11 Best chinese buffet I've had in Clearwater area, and I've eaten here for years at all hours with family and friends, and brought staff here for private meals in the large side dining/meeting room that can be closed off. The food quality is always very good for a buffet, with a wide variety of dishes that are refreshed regularly. They have cold boiled shrimp, and some sushi choices (it's far from the best sushi I've ever had, but better than most buffet sushi I've tasted). Restaurant interior is very nice and clean, and service is consistently prompt and attentive. The restaurant is temporarily closed right now for upgrades (the sign outside says they're adding a hibachi grill), but should reopen very soon. Give 'em a call to make sure they're open. If you're in the mood for a chinese buffet, definitely check it out. My scores, based on a "buffet scale" are: Atmosphere: 4 Food: 4 Service: 4 Value: 5

text: I can't believe how neglected this hotel is. First off let me just say that every hotel staff person I interacted with was friendly and helpful, especially the woman who was in charge of the breakfast buffet. That said, this is the dingiest hotel I have ever stayed in: Once you step inside your nostrils are assaulted by the smell of pungent chlorine. It smells like a chemical shed next to a pool! When I got to my room I noticed that the blankets on both of the beds had numerous cigarette burns on them. Gross! Also the knob in the shower has the "H" and "C" on the wrong sides- one morning I was in a hurry but could not bring myself to have a cold shower. Later I discovered that the temperature labels were installed wrong. They do have a complimentary breakfast and it's okay. The breakfast room has a large t.v. I used the exercise room one morning and it's small but it served my purposes. The treadmill there is ancient and doesn't slow down when you press "stop" it just stops! I almost fell off. Dear hotel owner: Fix the rank chlorine smell, replace your ratty old cigarette burnt blankets, fix your mislabeled showers, and also spray for bugs- I saw a stink bug crawling on some of the fake flowers while I was waiting for my elevator. This place is highly neglected. It's depressing. I feel sorry for the nice people who work there (except the ones responsible for all this negligence.)

text: Well, I returned as I said I would. On this second -- and final -- visit, the owner got in her own way. She stopped by the table to welcome us (good start) but then lecture around her food philosophy. Her heart is absolutely in the right place and, like another reviewer said, she means well. However, her almost obnoxious overtaking of our dining experience to insult every other Mexican-food experience (including that of my home state, Cali) was absolutely off-putting and unnecessary. As for the food this visit, I went specifically to try the menudo, available weekends only and a rare find in South Tampa. A really great example of how the above "situation" with the owner played out was: (after a lecture about why she charges for chips and salsa -- OK, I get it already) I asked if their menudo had hominy in it. Simple question. First, she was taken aback that I'd ordered menudo. (Gasp, you put something on your menu no one in the area would dare try?) After that, I got an earful about how hominy in menudo is not "real menudo" and about how where she's from, they'd NEVER put hominy in menudo. OK, thanks. I like hominy in my menudo, but I'm also fine without it. What I don't like is the commentary given to ANY customer around how their taste preference is off/wrong/incorrect or otherwise not acceptable. As for the actual menudo, it was only OK. It needed the hominy. ;-) Advice: As much as I'd usually recommend otherwise, in this case, I suggest that you keep the owner off the floor, train the servers well, and just let them do their job. I won't be back.
label: NEG

text: We ordered a steak, pepperoni, and mushroom stromboli. antipasto salad, and onion rings. The stromboli was very good. It was missing a side of marinara sauce but they gave some upon request. They did however charge us for onions in the stromboli which was not ordered. The biggest complaint was the antipasto salad. It was supposed to have crisp lettuce, ham, artichoke hearts, salami, provolone, tuna, hard boiled egg, and green olives. The only ingredients from that list were the lettuce. The rest were NOT there. It had cucumber, grape tomatoes, roasted red peppers, black olives with pits, prosciutto and mozzarella. I do not know what that salad was but it was not antipasto salad. And it was no bigger than a dinner salad but we were charged $9.75. BTW, the onion rings were good. I am going to continue to go to Vitarellis in Cherry Hill which is only two miles away and they have great stromboli and antipasto salad. P.S. - I called the restaurant and discussed the salad situation. Apparently there are two antipasto on the menu - one under the salad category and one under the appetizer category. Unless you read every line in the entire menu, a customer does not know this. And why is there a salad in the appetizer category? We did not know that this duplication existed. Even though we ordered the antipasto salad we apparently received the antipasto appetizer. Restaurants should not have two items on the menu with same name. They should have also clarified which one I was ordering because of the duplication - this did not happen. They know that this problem exists so it is the servers responsibility to clarify. Both the restaurant owner and restaurant manager tried to make excuses for the problem blaming an old menu, time of day, and other excuses. This is poor customer appreciation. Just know that if you want antipasto salad make it perfectly clear. Me - I am going elsewhere. It is just not worth the hassle.

text: When my friends suggested we go here for opening night, I was very excited. Twisted Tail sounded like a great little place for some well cooked pig and the whiskey/bourbon bar would be a bonus. I arrived a little after my party, was greeted and served a drink in a very timely manner and the cocktails were all mixed deliciously. I really enjoyed the Black Cherry Gimlet (...not trying to be miss know it all, but mixing a vodka/gin drink with lime juice does not a gimlet make) and the Time after Thyme. Service in this place is great. As far as the menu, to say I was disappointed to be at a place that clearly referenced swine in the name but has a total of three menu choices with pig (one has sausage, one has bacon, and the last seems like a pork shoulder) is an understatement. I also can't figure out what made anything on the menu consistent. Crawfish mac and cheese, duck spring rolls, flatbread and onion tarts... what? I got a salad and fries, because I'm on a diet... (not really.) and all of my friends ordered various appetizers. I know I should have ordered off of the entrees menu, but I wasn't really hungry and my friends and I tend to share anyway. The salad was good, but drenched in sweet dressing and the fries were good fries, but I feel like I paid $7 for a choice of three dipping sauces that were eh (chipotle ketchup, rosemary mayo, and agave nectar/vinegar). The crawfish mac and cheese was bland. The "spitfire chicken wings" were covered in a hoison glaze that tasted only of hoison glaze but had no semblance of cooked over an open fire (maybe it's a stretch to believe the wings were cooked over a fire, but it says SPITFIRE in the title). My friends liked their veggie options, but I didn't have any interest in trying any more food after the piece of crawfish I had was tough. After dinner, I tried to order some rye, but they were out of everything. The waiter explained "We just opened and some of these have been hard to find." And that was the final deal breaker for me. I get it, you just opened and the PA liquor board is full of Quakers or whatever, but print up new menus without teasing me. Will I come back? For the drinks, probably. The food, maybe if they pick up some herbs and spices and find some flavor.
label: NEG

text: My reply is to Charlie B.'s from Philadelphia Certainly very accurate description of the coffee beans process, toasting etc. but he is missing a big point: the ultimate product. I am italian grew up in Italy where espresso probably has longer history than here. Yes we italian are much less cerebral than here in US where you can write book about coffee. We just go to a bar for a good espresso or cappuccino prepared quickly. Here it has become (no judging) a ritual. Said this I did try the Bodhi's and Spruce Street 's espresso, in both places the time to wait for a coffee is unbelievable long, price outrageously expensive. Maybe the trendy and very expensive Stumptown beans are perfect for hand poured coffee but certainly not for espresso I can tell you this much, those beans are way to bitter. Bottom line La Colombe offers the best coffee beans for espresso and cappuccino prepared in a short time with no wait as many of my italian friends agree on. All baristas there are top of the line and I am talking not so much about the decoration with the foam (they are very good of course) but the efficiency and fast service they provide no matter how long the line is. For what regards the owners of La Colombe I honestly don't care much of what they do with their personal lives as far as they run a good business !!! In terms of dates form roasting he is correct , coffee should be consumed within 2 weeks from grounding but with the big sale they have I don't think that is an issue and even when you buy coffee in Torrefazione in Italy they don't put the date. One last point if you make homemade espresso you know that coffee machine should keep a little residual of coffee grinds. As a matter of fact when you buy a coffee machine in Italy they always suggest to run for few time to condition the machine. I hope this was helpful ! Paola C.
label: POS

text: Just went to Carpinteria for the day last weekend for the parks 80th anniversary celebration. So much to see in the park I spent more time walking around looking at things. It was a minus tide, first time I've been at Carp when the tide was so low and WOW! What amazing tidepools! See http://www.caopenspace.org/carpinteria.html for a few tidepool pics from last Sat (2/18/12). I walked the beach, past Jelly Bowl and Tar Pit Park to the Carpinteria Seal Sanctuary, lots of Harbor Seals and their pups. This is about the only place publically accessible in Southern California to see a seal rookery. A new creek mouth restoration was just completed too, included a lot of pretty native plants (which in the spring when things bloom should look even nicer). I've put this one on my "must camp" list, I like the spots practically right on the sand next to the creek mouth, I bet that would be really peaceful at night.

text: I realize I am not in the majority here and I may be committing seppuku by ripping on local, beloved favorite but yes, I am going to go there. I have been to Pop Shop three times now. I am not a believer of monstrous portions for my buck, especially when it's average. Time #3, we had what is supposedly the best thing here, the grilled cheese whatnot. My husband had the Bobby Flay special, which was average. Not bad but if I was a celeb chef I wouldn't put my name on it. It was paired with a cup of tomato soup that was worth the $1 and change charge. It was blah. I had the montecristo grilled cheese but it was not a stand out for me. I don't get why people flock to this place and wait for 30+ minutes. I wouldn't. Now don't get me wrong, if this is your kind of thing then it's great. It's great to take your kids if you have em, and the nuggets have fun there and it shows. Another thing is it is very loud in there, think school cafeteria with balloons and ice cream. text: After eating at Panera today I knew I had to give my 2 cents worth on Yelp. Yes, I too have eaten at Panera Bread in other cities. Some people were just standing around reading the menu, and others, like me, thought they were in line. Not until someone pointed out there were 4 cashiers and to just go to any of them did I realize there was no organization. I placed my order with a young woman who was void of personality or assistance. Once I received my buzzer I found a table and went to retrieve my drink. And that is when the frustration really kicked into gear. Within an area approximately five feet wide and five feet long was the soft dtink dispenser, all condiments from salt, pepper, utinsils, mustard, mayo and ketchup packets, lids, straws, lemons, etc. etc. On the opposite wall of this shoebox configuration was where the employees emptied the dirty dishes and disposed of the plates, bowls, etc. In order to get your food you had to walk through this area where no less than 5 people (customers, employees) were trying to do whatever they needed to do. I first went for my drink, and had to manipulate around others. My second visit was to pick up my order and once again I had to dodge several people to retrieve my food, and then I had to turn around and immediately fight back through this disorganized group with my food. My third and most dreaded visit was when I realized I had forgotten to get condiments. I dreaded the necessary visit! I left thinking that their food in no way warranted going through such chaos again. Whoever designed this paticular Panersa Bread should be fired! No, I will not return!

But it's hard to enjoy anything when you can't move. Raven packs in people like Lil Wayne packs in bowls. Turning your neck involves saying "excuse me" to three people. Gangster-ass gangster rap thumped most of the night in lieu of fun, dumb pop and hip hop. Even without the space restraint you can bust nary a move here. It's the kind of music you just stand around trying to look cool to. I don't know if I see my picture in the corner, but that's a lot of work for me. There's a huge opportunity here for another place to show these folks how a bar should be run. You wouldn't have to try too hard at all! text: Guess what? Back in the old days places would run out of stuff! Why? Because they made it fresh, because they did not want to have left overs because they did not serve left overs the second (or the Xth) day. Businesses had personality, and sometimes because the city the place is in is business hostile establishments didn't have nice big easy to see signs, so places were not as easy to find as we have grown accustomed to in the 21st century consumer America. Everything old is new again or whatever other trite expression ya want - Mrs. Izenberg made us some great turkey sandwiches - a delicious turkey club with bacon freshly cooked to order and a traditional turkey on rye with cole slaw and russian. Yeah I got cheese on it as the photos show but that was not to besmirch my cred ("corned beef on white bread with, uh, mayonnaise and tomatoes and lettuce." (extra credit for those under 30 who can cite the reference w/o using google!)) but to try the cheese which was good quality as opposed to the yellow crap some places try to get away with. It was good BTW - Cooper Sharp I think. Mrs. Izenberg told us that they were out of brisket just like Tom's troubles in the previous review. She told us we needed to come back and try it, and judging from our two superb sandwiches, a nice Levis hot dog on a great roll this place makes great stuff for reasonable prices for the quality and quantity you get. http://www.levishotdogs.com/ (not Levi's as in the jeans and the long gone NYC rye bread BTW as Mrs. Izenberg corrected me with a winning smile) We did have less then great fries - they had those thin real french fries just like you get in France - kind of like potato sticks - I like thick fries better and so does Mrs. Izenberg - she said they don't keep much stock and last time they went to their supplier they were out of the thick fries so they got the shoe strings - Mrs. Izenberg assured me she would have their standards back in next time I came by! I think this place is great and will be back soon!

text: I hardly ever write reviews, usually just rely on others to help me make decisions...but I HAD to write this one. I decided to try out Tierra Mia based on Yelp reviews, and I am so happy that I did! I went for my first Brazilian wax, and of course I was very nervous (aka terrified). However, as soon as I walked in I felt welcomed and comfortable. Since it was my ever Brazilian wax (or any type of wax for that matter!) Karina took the time to explain exactly what would happen, what it might feel like, and what to expect afterwards. She even told me what to watch out for if I go to a different salon/spa for a waxing (double dipping etc.), which I feel is a pretty rare custom! In the beginning I felt pretty self-conscious and nervous but Karina made me feel comfortable. Ok now for my take on the pain...you are putting wax on your skin and ripping out every little hair so of course it is going to hurt...but it really wasn't that bad! I don't in any way have a high tolerance for pain so I was expecting to be in agony, but it wasn't that way at all. Some sections hurt more than others, which Karina warned me about ahead of time, so she would have me take deep breaths when she got to those areas. I think it also helps to not take any rest between sections, otherwise you have time to lay there and think about the pain-better to get it all done with quickly! Overall, my experience was great and the price was comparable to other salons in the area so I have since gone back for a maintenance and just scheduled another.
label: POS

text: So I checked out Yelp before I going to Eulogy and the reviews ring true. Now I am no beer connoisseur nor beer snob - but I like the stuff and I want to try more beers even learn a bit more about it. So here's the jist from a 'beer likers' point of view: Walking in there were a few people at the bar and at the few tables - very respectable for a Sunday evening. There may have been a more sizable crowd upstairs but I did not check it out. The space downstairs was laid back and looked just like a beer tavern should: low lighting, dark wood, long bar, tall bar stools. Chris behind the bar was very kind and patient with my perusing of the beer menu. He was able to come around periodically and offer suggestions. Ten minutes later when I decided what type of beer I wanted to try (no judging - the choices are endless) Chris gave me a couple of suggestions, one sample and led me happily to my perfect choice. I enjoyed the rest of my evening comfortably chillin and sipping on my well chosen beer. To cap off a great experience Chris even gave a mini science lesson when I asked what I felt rolling in a can of beer. Turns out it was a floating widget - used to release liquid nitrogen and provide better head quality!! So now I know --- I sound kinda beer snobbish right?? I will definitely be heading back - several times over.

text: Come here for a magical evening... The Harbor Restaurant is located on the wharf in Santa Barbara. The view is lovely and there is valet parking. I have only ever been here for dinner and I always reserve a table with a view. For lunch, I go upstairs to Longboards. The service is good and the drinks are yummy. I love a margarita or a nice bottle of White Zinfandel (depending on what you order) and for a nice after dinner drink, I enjoy their heavenly "raspberry truffle". They have a wide variety of seafood and I have always enjoyed my dinners here. Delicious clam chowder and generous shrimp cocktails are my appetizers of choice. For the main course, I particularly recommend the seared ahi tuna or the Australian lobster tail, but really everything is good here. The one complaint I have is that my favorite dish (giant Alaskan king crab legs served warm as a main course) was taken off the menu. They still serve crab legs cold, but in a seafood platter. However, if they're not busy and you get a nice waiter they will sometimes still make it for you. I always give a more generous tip when they do. I recommend the Harbor Restaurant for dates and for people visiting Santa Barbara for the first time. I would not recommend this restaurant for families with small children.

text: I don't get the reviews of Perch Pub???????? Mel and I were happy to finally visit. The reviews are so good on Yelp. I have to assume most were written by friends or by the staff themselves. I mean exactly the same as the places mentioned above.....and more expensive then I'm used to seeing. I had nachos that were just ok. They use better chips than most places, but try to disguise the small amount of meat, and veg by slathering a ton of cheese whiz over everything. Mel had fish tacos that were pretty good but really small for $5.00 per taco. we tried a couple of sides and were underwhelmed all over. The beer list is good, but again....there are a dozen other places I could get the same list. Give me something...focus on a couple of specific breweries, give me a special price to try something different, give me a tasting option....for god sakes take a risk somewhere. The booze. Whiskey village looks generous in comparison! {That is not an endorsement of WV..they are far too short with their pour as well}. Before you go back to Perch Pub go back to or try: Varga Bar, Devil's Den, Royal Tavern, Race Street Tavern, Good Dog, Ten Stone, Sidecar, Pub & Kitchen, Misconduct. text: Central Grocery is home of the muffuletta, one of New Orleans' greatest culinary inventions. The hefty sandwich is quartered and wrapped and sold ready to go ... or to unwrap immediately and eat along the counters that have been installed at the back of the store. In our opinion, this mighty muffuletta (available as a half sandwich) is the best and ONLY muffuletta to eat period. Yes, other restaurants now have versions of it, but this big fella has a classic dignity that simply cannot be beat. And the store, while a smidgen less quaint then it used to be, and no longer a full-service sandwich shop (muffulettas are the only meal you can get), is still a fine place to shop. It is the same well-weathered, creaky-floored emporium it has been for decades, its grocery shelves a wonderland for all who like pickles, olives, peppers, and spice. What has not changed one bit is Central Grocery's distinct aroma: an irresistibly appetizing perfume of salamis, cheeses, garlic, and oil. text: As much as I have frequented this library over the years (many times!), the Central Branch of the Free LIbrary doesn't seem to live up to what it's supposed to be: The main hub of the Philadelphia free library system. What I mean is that they've done a lot of renovating over the past few years - the majority of which hasn't been beneficial to the library or the public. They redesigned the Music section, taking away the turntables and vinyl records to make room for (more) cds (believe it or not, many people still like vinyl). (Although I see they've sneaked in a few turntables recently.) They've also ditched alot of old sheet music and have even more sheet music that remains uncatalogued (due to the lack of funds and staff). Their main lending room, Philbrick Lending Library, has also been redesigned. They've managed to move multiple copies of books and put them in their respective sections (some books were in the Philosophy, Education, and Religion room while another copy was in the Philbrick room, so putting things in one place made sense), but they've put in Self-Checkout stations there and in the main lobby (where lots of people just stare at the screen figuring out what to do while the staff offers little to no help - that is, if they're even around to offer little help). And you cannot check out cds and dvds at those stations. You still have to go up to the counter and get a staffer for that. Two other big minuses: One, the reduction of hours in the Newspaper Department. That now closes three hours before the rest of the library (on late nights). It seems to me the library's main focus is yuppy Wi-Fi and the computers with their ultra-high speed connections. Second: The change machines that do not make change for anything other than one dollar bills. The machines briefly took five dollar bills and that suddenly stopped. That was convenient, so why not go back to that? It would help those of us who still like (or have) to make copies. (And try to make change for anything above a five in the cafe). Speaking of the cafe, it's nice enough, but a bit pricey. They have a nice selection of food and junk (what would Philadelphia be without our beloved junk food?), but they need to brew someone other than corporate, overrated, bitter Starbucks coffee. Their coffee sucks, 'nuff said On the plus side: The Government Publications Department has some decent document and microfilm holdings (census reels from 1790-1920, minus, of course, 1890; Philadelphia death returns 1803-1860, to name a few). Their Rare Book Department is underrated and doesn't have enough of hours to display the gems they have. One last thing: If you're looking for language instruction tapes and cds, their collection is pathetic and outdated. The place to go for that would be the Andorra Branch (located on upper Henry Avenue), or simply request the materials be transferred from that branch. And the place to go for decent movies and music is the Chestnut Hill branch (on upper Germantown Avenue). (Why the best stuff is located in branches that are almost out of the city is "interesting.") And there are interesting people and smells here, but this IS Center City, after all. The better action is at the branch libraries. BTW: All lectures and book signings are not free. The bigger names are charging as much as $35 for tickets - and, naturally, the more well-known the author is, the better the chances that you're going to be looking at their lecture on closed-circuit TV in the lobby get (in other words, why bother going if that's the case?). Despite all these criticisms, I do love this library, but improvements are needed to really make this the true gem of the city's library system.

We clearly ate more than $50 worth (not hard when Lamb Saag will put you back $25) knowing that we had $100 on the card. We started to argue and he literally pushed the receipt in our face. At this point he was getting really aggressive so I just gave him my credit card for the remaining $20. It doesn't stop there. Then he corners my husband after he's coming out of the bathrooms. (The bathrooms are really awkward by the way. The door to the bar faces the bathroom so while I washed my hands, bar patrons were watching. Creepy.) Anyway, he corners my husband (corners him!) and follows him back to our table and says, "This is from 2007." 2007? The event was in November 2010! In the end we said, "This is none of our concern. text: My experience with LifeShield was one of the worst experiences I've ever had with any vendor. The system LefeShield sent me simply didn't work, and their technicians couldn't make it work. Despite these problems, they initially refused to cancel the three-year contract. It took an inordinate amount of time on the phone and the following letter to get the matter resolved. Dear Sir/Madam: My LifeShield home security system was shipped to me on July 1, 2011, and I installed it and started using it shortly after it arrived. At first, the system seemed to function normally. On August 25, 2011, local police showed up at my home, because they received a call from your monitoring service. After following up with your support staff, I learned that the alarm was triggered because after arming, the system did not detect that the door was closed when we left our home. Your support staff offered no solution to the problem. After another false alarm, your support staff indicated that I had an older model door sensor which was prone to malfunctions caused by vibrations when the door was closed. You sent me a new sensor. Installing the new sensor made no difference. After the next false alarm, your support staff tried resetting various parts of the system. Their efforts were fruitless. Several false alarms followed. Again, I followed up with your support staff. No solution was offered, and one of your representatives indicated that if I was not satisfied with your service, I should cancel my account. On September 11, I placed a call to request cancellation of my account and refund of payments made so far. The agent who took the call indicated that he needed to have the cancellation approved by his manager. While I was on the phone, the agent informed me that after reviewing my history, the manager approved the cancellation, that the account would be cancelled, and that I would be receiving a shipping slip I could use to return the system. When I asked about payments made so far, the agent informed me that the manager would call me to discuss the matter. I didn't hear from the manager until September 14 despite several messages left on his voicemail. By the time the manager got in touch with me, he had apparently changed his mind about canceling my account. Instead, he put me in touch with a senior technician. The technician verified that my sensor was installed properly and suggested a slight tweak to the installation. The technician's suggestion made no difference. I left messages for both the technician and the manager several days ago and have not heard from either of them. It's clear that the system you sold me is defective. The sensor is highly unreliable. It intermittently fails to detect when the door is opened and closed, as evidenced by the messages on the console, the feedback chimes and, of course, the false alarms. The nature of the problems renders the system unusable, and I have stopped trying to use it to protect my home. Since I am still without a functioning system after more than 60 days, and you are unable to rectify the problems, despite your technicians' repeated attempts to troubleshoot the issues with the current and the original sensors, please cancel my account and send me a refund for the payments made to date.
